extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history; connoisseurs and critics of sculpture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for judging ancient Greek sculpture—technical execution, materials, style, subject-matter, and expressive qualities—with examples drawn from Aegina, Myron, Polycleitus, and funerary monuments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical excellence / mastery of tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Execution with an application of all known instruments of sculpture; delicate calculation of weight in composition allowing figures to stand with minimal supports; bold use of the chisel; fineness of execution even in parts invisible to ordinary spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the sculptor's control of technique (weight distribution, plinth thinness, chisel work to thinnesses of a few inches, and meticulous finish). Example: Overbeck's praise of Aegina marbles for dispensing with artificial supports and finishing invisible parts. Anti-pattern: crude or structurally insecure compositions that rely on obvious supports or lack refined tool-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and ideal of the unveiled human form
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hellenic (Dorian/European) value in art of the unveiled, healthy human form as an element of temperance, preferring the undraped body over gaudy Asiatic ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether nudity is used to embody temperance and the Hellenic spirit rather than mere decoration; example: Aeginetan warriors shown nude to embody the Hellenic ideal, with only Paris retaining ornate trappings. Anti-pattern: over-ornamentation that subordinates human form to exotic detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material choice and awareness (marble vs bronze)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of white Parian marble as suited to severity of thought, yet with reminiscences of bronze in slimness and poised grouping; awareness of the differing structural possibilities of bronze (hollow casting) vs marble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how material is chosen and exploited: marble's cool massiveness vs bronze's capacity for lighter balancing. Note deliberate cross-medium effects (slimness suggesting bronze) and attachments of metal accessories. Anti-pattern: neglecting material constraints leading to awkward poses or unsupported projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited and conventionalised use of colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Traces of colour found on marbles—outer shields and helmets blue, inner parts and crests red, gilding for scale-work, coloured eyes and lips—indicating a restrained, conventional application of polychromy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence of coloured surfaces and whether colour is applied sparingly for conventional emphasis (edges, crests, drapery hems) rather than full polychromy. Example: gilding for Paris's scale armour. Anti-pattern: anachronistic expectation of pure white marble without recognising original polychrome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of metal accessories with marble work
rubrics_metrics.description: Metal actually mingled with marble via attachments (little holes for lances, swords, bows, Medusa on the aegis), enriching detail and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appraise presence and quality of mixed-media attachments and how they enhance realism and detail. Example: drilled holes in Aegina marbles for bronze fittings. Anti-pattern: ignoring original metal elements when reconstructing or interpreting the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos and humane expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of natural, pathetic effect and true humanity—figures showing yearning, grief, or tender attention—contrasted with the hardness and cruelty of oriental art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work's capacity to evoke genuine emotional response (e.g., a figure leaning to the fallen leader); prefer works that embody Homeric sensibility of pity and tenderness. Anti-pattern: emotionally flat or purely formulaic processions lacking individual feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful expression of pain and suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigid expression of the truth of pain (e.g., recumbent figure with lips open, hard-shut lips of Hercules) as evidence of technical and expressive maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fidelity and force of depictions of pain—do they convincingly convey physical agony without sentimentality? Example: eastern gable's stronger handling of pain. Anti-pattern: melodramatic or schematic depictions that undercut authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, naïveté, and freshness in immature art
rubrics_metrics.description: Early or immature art can possess attractiveness in naïveté: freshness of spirit, simple motives of feeling, and pleasure in mechanical processes performed with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and value simple readiness, charm of limitations, and unforced composition (e.g., designer making two spearmen kneel to fill space). Do not penalise all 'arrested' technique—look for genuine freshness. Anti-pattern: equating lack of polish with failure when there is evident vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal composition and rhythmic balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact and formal correspondences between parts, careful composition to fill space, and a learned sense of balance (including the two gables’ correspondence and the arranged kneeling figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge compositional economy and the balancing of figures within architectural constraints; excellence includes successful filling of space without awkwardness. Anti-pattern: compositions that betray spatial incompetence or arbitrary figure placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical proportion and evolving typology
rubrics_metrics.description: Profiles and body proportions vary with development: earlier works show sharp prominence of nose and chin and archaically slim shoulders; later works approach fully developed Greek type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proportional realism relative to period conventions—recognise archaic traits as period-appropriate rather than strictly 'errors'. Example: Aeginetan profiles compared with later Attic types. Anti-pattern: judging archaic proportions by later classical standards without historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of animation and lifelikeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures convey true expression of life and animation—stiff grace combined with direct felt emotion, producing a sense of living presence comparable to Homer or Chaucer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise works that communicate movement, internal life, or vivid presence even within conventional or formal constraints. Anti-pattern: technically accurate but lifeless figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural function and ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture conceived as architectural ornament—limitations of the medium emphasise its function as part of a structure (e.g., Hermes Kriophorus in a niche), with hieratic, stiff, and formal qualities appropriate to that role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sculpture within its intended architectural role; measure success by how well ornamentation serves structural and visual integration rather than freestanding narrative. Anti-pattern: treating architectural reliefs as if they were independent monumental sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funerary/commemorative purpose and realism of portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Funeral monuments often present vivid, selected pages of daily life—portraits or likenesses preserving memory of the dead (e.g., Trypho), combining personal feeling with public commemoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for convincing individualized detail and domestic cues that render commemorative works socially informative and artistically successful. Anti-pattern: generic or impersonal funerary figures lacking memorial specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism and readable narrative imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of symbolic imagery (e.g., sirens carrying shrouded souls, goddess figures of life and death) to convey beliefs about death and renewal, often with conventional motifs adapted persuasively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity and persuasiveness of symbolic program: are symbols used coherently and do they communicate intended ideas? Example: Harpy Tomb's siren-figures likely representing souls. Anti-pattern: ambiguous or muddled symbolism that obscures intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject selection: athletic youth and civic ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Predominant subject-matter of the athletic age is youthful bodies in gymnastic discipline, celebrating civic pride, family, and moral/intellectual values attached to athletic victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether subject choice (prizemen, athletes) aligns with cultural ideals and is rendered with appropriate dignity and idealisation (e.g., Diadumenus, Discobolus). Anti-pattern: trivialising prize-subjects or failing to convey civic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism in natural detail and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithful and observant depiction of tactile details—hair locks, tense nerves, veins, the rhythmus of motion—yielding a convincing counterfeit of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the accuracy and sensitivity of small details as evidence of close study; excellence manifests in convincing texture and anatomical specificity. Anti-pattern: superficial or schematic detailing that betrays lack of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between bodily (anima) and mental (animus) expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sculptors (e.g., Myron) excel in expressing the animal/physical soul (movement, bodily perfection) while giving little expression to the reasonable mind or inner sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating facial expression and psychological depth, distinguish deliberate restraint (to preserve youthful physical ideal) from artistic limitation; judge whether suppression of mental expression serves the work's purpose. Anti-pattern: misreading a lack of 'mind' as simply technical failure when it may be stylistic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of the interplay of motion and repose
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to capture the mystery of combined motion and rest—'rest in motion'—so that a figure seems poised between opposed movements (e.g., Discobolus capturing a moment between the backward swing and forward throw).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate timing, tension, and equilibrium in the pose; excellence makes the frozen moment feel dynamically plausible. Anti-pattern: static poses that lack internal tension or contrived, unintelligible contortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of copies, restorations, and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness that many extant works are copies, restorations, or later reproductions which may alter style or authenticity; variations of copyists/restorers can mislead judgments of originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor provenance, copy-status, and restoration history into assessments; compare multiple versions when possible (e.g., discobolus variants at British Museum and Palazzo Massimi). Anti-pattern: relying on a single, heavily-restored example as the definitive standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate learned complexity subordinated to visual purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate or contorted manner may be learned and intricate, but should be subordinated to the primary visual purpose (to be looked at rather than thought about); naturalness succeeding despite learned involution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works where technical or rhetorical virtuosity serves immediate visual effect rather than obscures it. Example: Quintilian's description of Discobolus' learned involution yet effective naturalness. Anti-pattern: complexity for its own sake that distracts from the viewer's perception.
